this week visit someone who is lonely or who lives alone. do thirtieth sunday in ordinary time the word year a 25 october 2026 colour: green psalter week 2 the pharisees prided themselves on strict observance of the law. so meticulous were they in keeping it, they had worked out that the biblical law contained 365 negative commandments (one ‘thou shalt not’ for every day of the year) and 248 positive commandments (one for every bone in the human body). in addition to this written law, they believed that god had given moses another set of laws that weren’t written down but were passed down by an unbroken chain from moses to them. some pharisees taught that every commandment was to be observed with the same attention to detail. others taught that the commandments ranged from serious to relatively minor. this debate provides the background to today’s gospel. by asking jesus’ opinion, his opponents are also inviting him to line up on one side or the other in the debate. jesus answers by quoting a verse from the book of deuteronomy that every member of his audience would know (dt. 6:5). it was part of the prayer they said twice each day, the shema yisrael (‘hear , o israel, the lord our god is he then adds a verse that ‘resembles this’ – the command to love your neighbour as yourself (leviticus 18:2). on these two verses, he says, hang the whole of the law and the prophets, that is, god’s entire revelation to his people. this is the law that matters. n love, only love mt 22:34-40 we use the word ‘love’ with easy abandon today. think of the casual way we throw it around. we love our bed, our favourite tv soap, our new shoes. we love salt with our chips, sugar in our tea, and a trip to the cinema. i love everything that’s bad for me, according to my cardiologist. love is desire, obsession, addiction, commitment, lust, service; love is whatever we want it to be. but if we christians want to know what love truly is, we need only look to god. god is love, st john tells us. god not only loves, god is love. and where there is love, there is god. in her book reading genesis, marilynne robinson points out that this godly love is what distinguished the god of israel from other middle eastern gods of antiquity. the babylonians and others believed in multiple gods; abraham and his descendants were unique in being monotheists, in believing there is but one god, who had created them in god’s very own image. we are not images of angels or lesser gods but of the creator himself. this was a radical way of thinking. the other gods of antiquity were remote, distant, and indifferent to the happenings here on earth. the god of genesis is a benign god who forgives cain for the murder of his own brother, forgives his people time and again, and is personally invested in them, unlike the apathetic or vengeful gods that other peoples worshipped. israel’s god is slow to anger, rich in mercy, abiding in love. god, robinson says, has a lofty view of humankind, expressed poetically in psalm 8: “what is man that you are mindful of him?yet you have made him a little lower than the heavenly beings and crowned him with glory and honour .” god loves, and god is love. but, when we say this, we’re not describing an up in the sky kind of love. we’re describing the kind of concrete love that jesus showed. people practise this kind of love every day. think of parents who care for children with special needs. or grandparents who pick up the pieces when their child’s marriage collapses. or groups like the st vincent de paul, who help the most needy. all of these put love into practice every day. i like to break down the great commandment into its three parts. we are to:* love ourselves. healthy self-love comes from knowing i am made in god’s own image. healthy self-love is not the same as selfishness or narcissism. it is to see myself the way god sees me, as one made in god’s own image. therefore, i am unique, lovable, irreplaceable. many of us find it hard to love ourselves. young people, influenced by social media, find it so hard to love themselves. but if we are to love god and others, we must learn to love ourselves. love our neighbour. to love is to will the good of another. it is to go out of our way for others. “feed the poor .” that’s love. “break bread with those no one will sit with.” that’s love. “respond with patience to someone who gets on my nerves.” that’s love. love of neighbour means never being bystanders. more than anything else, god will judge us on whether we loved others. love god. god created us out of love, and sustains us lovingly each day. we return god’s love through a life of prayer, worship and good works. st paul instructed the ephesians to ‘live a life of love.’ three little words beginning with the letter l. easy to remember. hard to do. that’s how we keep the great commandment. n reflectsay “lord, help me to love you and my neighbour to the best of my ability.” pray for your parish community, that all will grow in love of god and one another. pray love of god and neighbour is the mark of the christian at the heart of our faith is that knowledge that god loves us without reservation learn son, using somewhat less diplomatic language to explain that pope francis would be very displeased with his ac - tions. he agreed to call his boss who clearly had a better understanding of what was at stake. the survivors were ushered into the residence where some young nuns served refreshments. this helped to ease the tension in the group who were understandably upset at having been left waiting in the cars. the group bonded quickly. seven of the eight were happy to be identified, but the eighth person asked not to be, a wish that was honoured by the others. they also agreed to meet with the pope as a group, which made for a much better use of the available time. pope francis arrived at the nunciature at about 5.10 and the meeting commenced within five minutes. there was another meeting scheduled to take place after the meeting with the survivors, after which pope francis was due at the festival of the families in croke park. there was not a lot of time. pope francis went into the meeting with the eight survivors and an interpreter. an hour passed and those waiting outside the room wondered whether this was a good sign or not. with - thought for the week “our goal must be infinite, not the finite. the infinite is our homeland: heaven has been waiting for us forever.” (st. carlo acutis.) reflection – 24th / 25th october, 2026 in our world today we see lots of aggressive behaviour towards many groups of people. we are witnessing a rise in racist attacks, on individua ls who are different - culturally, economically, religiously and ethnically. our ownci ties and towns have had many such episodes, some people being left horribly injured and others fatally wounded. we were always regarded as a welcoming, safe and hospitab le nation but in recent decades these qualities have been seriously tested. can never presume again that we are the once renowned land of a thousand welc omes. yet there is an innate generosity, kindness and compassion in our hearts as an irish nation, qualities evident in our own parishioners and community. we have a deep generosity. in today’s first reading, the israelites are commanded “to love the stranger.” they are to look into their hearts and remember the time when they were the outsiders . loving the stranger was the right thing to do because it’s what god expected . when we give hospitality to people in need they cease being strangers or outsiders. thus, hospitality became a primary virtue. for the nomadic israelite people, hospitality literally became a matter o f life and death: travellers depended for their survival on the hospitality of stra ngers. anyone outside their own natural setting or territory was seen as someone in need of special care. norms of respect, kindness and decency were laid down as to the way a stranger or anyone in need was to be treated. in the gospel jesus says, “you must love your neighbour as yourself.” he is speaking to all of us. as the israelites were asked to love the strange r, so too, as christians, we are asked to do likewise. the ultimate offer of hospitali ty is genuine love, a love that attaches no conditions to our compassionate respon se to those in need. pope leo has said, “love with christ’s compassionate heart.” he invites us to move from a culture of indifference towards active, frat ernal closeness. our love for one another is to be rooted in god’s uncond itional love for us. saint mother theresa said , “the fruit of love is service which is compassion in action. intense love does not measure, it just gives.” we have a great legacy of saints in our church’s history who have taught us what unconditional love and compassion are. they exemplified the sacrificial and compassion of jesus. they lived his way of loving, giving, caring, being compassionate, generous of spirit. they all had a willingness to alwa ys be there for the stranger, the outcast, the hurt, broken and wounded. let us remember the command of jesus this coming week: love one another – but always in imitation of him. beginning today. when we respond caringly to one another, we have the assurance that we minister to christ. “ i was a stranger and you welcomed me.”fr tony crumlin

god with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind.” and “you shall love your neighbour as yourself.” this brief exchange is found in all three synoptic gospels (mark 12:28-31 and luke 10:25- 28). we can also say that st john’s gospel focuses on love. in fact, it is said that when st john was an old man he would always emphasise the importance of love. scripture scholars tell us that there are 613 commandments in the hebrew bible and there was a discussion among the rabbis as to which of them were the most important. the words of today’s gospel are helpful and consoling. lisieux, pope francis quoted her own words: “it is confidence and nothing but confidence that must lead us to love”. pope francis writes: “it is trust that brings us to love and thus sets us free from fear. it i s trust that helps us to stop looking to ourselves and enables us to put into god’s hands what he alone can accomplish”. he concludes, “at a time of great complexity, st therese can help us rediscover the importance of simplicity, the absolute primacy of love, trust and abandonment.” the cha llenge presented to us in today’s gospel is not easy. we have busy and demanding lifestyles when so many of us are juggling different work and family commitments. let us pray in the coming week let us ask god to help us to reach out to our neighbours with love wherever we may find them. st understanding the mass. the eucharistic prayer: "the heart of the mass" what the priest is doing everything in the mass has been moving towards this moment. the eucharistic prayer is the longest, most sacred prayer of the entire celebration the great act of thanksgiving through which bread and wine become the body and blood of christ. the priest alone speaks it, but he does not pray alone. he prays with the church, through christ, to the father, in the holy spirit. every word carries the weight of two thousand years of faith. at its centre comes the consecration the words of christ at the last supper at which point the bread and wine are truly transformed. how we should respond. this is not a moment for distraction or private prayer elsewhere. follow every word. the great "amen" that concludes the eucharistic prayer sometimes called the great amen is the congregation's ratification of everything the priest has prayed . it should be the most emphatic word we speak at mass. living this at mass at the consecration, when the priest elevates the host and then the chalice, look up. ( some of you may remember the late fr robinson encouraging you to do so as children all those years ago! ) the sacristan rings bells precisely to call our attention. this is the summit. be present to it completely. pope leoxiv prayer for the recovery of pope leo. loving and merciful god, we pray for our holy father, pope leo, asking you to bless him with healing, strength, and renewed health. be close to him in his time of need, grant him peace and comfort, and guide those who care for him. may he experience your loving presence and be restored to good health, so that he may continue to shepherd your church with wisdom and love. amen. masses 10 am monday to saturday, vigil mass saturday 6.30 pm sunday masses 9 am, 10.30 am, 12 noon . confessions after 10 am mass on saturday and on request baptisms on the 2nd saturday of each month at 2 pm. please contact the parish office contacts parish office 8316016 fr michael o’grady

“we are not the sum of our weaknesses and failures; we are the sum of the father’s love for us.” pope john paul thought for the week dates for your diary love of god that stops at the church door is incomplete. who is the stranger, widow or orphan waiting quietly for my love this week? to ponder this week the fundamental way of the church hymns 10.30am mass, church of the holy child, whitehall opening hymn no.8 closing hymn no.32 in matthew 22:34–40, jesus unifies the commandments to love god and neighbour. he reveals that these are not two separate paths, but an inseparable bond. true love of god (the vertical dimension) must immediately flow outward to our neighbour (the horizontal dimension). holy child nativity parishes beaumont | larkhill | whitehall | santry drawing from this exact relationship, the church's beloved holy father famously wrote in his first encyclical that "man is the primary and fundamental way for the church." he reminded us that because christ united himself to every human being, our devotion to the creator cannot be isolated from how we treat his creation. to truly love god means we must fiercely respect, defend, and cherish the sacred dignity of every single person. this call to love demands practical justice. in the first reading from exodus 22:20–26, god commands strict protection for the vulnerable—the stranger, the widow, and the orphan. mirroring this, the late pope consistently taught that a society is ultimately judged by how it treats its weakest members. loving our neighbour means ensuring the marginalised are never exploited. his sunday’s gospel brings us to the absolute core of our faith, providing a perfect opportunity to reflect a little on the legacy of saint john paul pope, whose feast day was celebrated this past thursday. year a | 30 sunday in ordinary time th
